questions.prompt: A torque wrench is calibrated to 40 N·m. A technician wants to know whether a used wrench still delivers 40 N·m on average. Which is the null hypothesis?
options: H₀: μ = 40 N·m, the mean torque of the wrench is still 40
H₀: μ ≠ 40 N·m, the mean torque of the wrench has changed
H₀: x̄ = 40 N·m, the sample mean of the readings is 40
H₀: μ > 40 N·m, the mean torque of the wrench is too high
questions.explanation: H₀ is the "nothing has changed" statement about the population mean μ, and it holds the equals sign. μ ≠ 40 is the alternative. A hypothesis is never about x̄: the sample mean is known once the readings are taken.

questions.prompt: A test on a bearing's mean diameter gives a p-value of 0.03. Which sentence says what 0.03 means?
options: If the mean really were on target, a sample this far off would happen about 3 % of the time
There is a 3 % probability that the mean diameter of the bearings is on target
There is a 97 % probability that the mean diameter of the bearings is off target
About 3 % of the bearings in the population have a diameter that is off target
questions.explanation: A p-value is computed assuming H₀ is true: it is the probability of a result at least this extreme under H₀. It is not the probability that H₀ is true or false, and it says nothing about the share of individual bearings.

questions.prompt: At α = 0.05 a test of H₀: μ = 12.0 mm gives p = 0.21. What should the report say?
options: Do not reject H₀: the data do not show that the mean differs from 12.0 mm
Accept H₀: the data prove that the mean is exactly 12.0 mm
Reject H₀: the data show that the mean differs from 12.0 mm
The test failed: a p-value above α means the test cannot be used
questions.explanation: p = 0.21 ≥ 0.05, so H₀ is not rejected. That means the evidence is not strong enough, as a "not guilty" verdict does; it does not prove the mean is exactly 12.0 mm. Nothing is wrong with the test.

questions.prompt: Match each courtroom outcome with its outcome in a hypothesis test.

pairs.right: Type I error: a true H₀ is rejected
Type II error: a false H₀ is not rejected
Correct: a false H₀ is rejected
Correct: a true H₀ is not rejected

questions.explanation: H₀ plays the part of "innocent". Rejecting it when it is true is a Type I error (its probability is α); failing to reject it when it is false is a Type II error (probability β). Item 8.6 treats both.

questions.prompt: A gauge has σ = 2 µm. Nine readings of a 500 µm standard average 501.4 µm. Test H₀: μ = 500 against H₁: μ ≠ 500. What is the z statistic? Give it to two decimals.
questions.explanation: The standard error is σ/√n = 2/√9 = 0.667 µm, so z = (501.4 − 500)/0.667 = 2.10. Its two-sided p-value is 2 × (1 − Φ(2.10)) = 0.0357, below 0.05: the gauge reads high. Dividing by σ instead would give 0.70.
